articles.title: Interest Rate Increases Are About Disciplining Labor
articles.author: Arthur MacEwan
articles.content_excerpt: Using its favored policy in the face of inflation, the Federal Reserve Board, under its new chairman, Kevin Warsh, pushed up short-term interest rates in September. This action may have some impact on the rate of inflation, but probably not much. Raising interest rates may curtail inflation under some circumstances, but the major factors bringing about the current, continuing inflation are unlikely to be much affected by the Fed’s recent interest rate increases. But those other factors are out of bounds: the Fed can’t alter them, and the current administration in Washington won’t. What Washington Has Done to Curtail Inflation With the emergence of economic instability in the early 1970s, President Richard Nixon imposed wage-price controls that limited how much wages and prices could rise.

articles.title: What Makes Somebody a Marxist?
articles.author: Vivek Chibber
articles.content_excerpt: Karl Marx famously declared that he was not a Marxist. But his theoretical work spawned many branches of research, political movements, and heated debate. Can we identify a set of unifying ideas that make up Marxism? On this latest episode of the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism , Vivek Chibber and Melissa Naschek look at the foundations of Marx’s writing and explain how Marxism has both developed and degenerated over the past century. Confronting Capitalism with Vivek Chibber is produced by Catalyst: A Journal of Theory and Strategy and published by Jacobin. You can listen to the full episode here . articles.title: The European Green Party Attacks Solidarity With Palestine
articles.author: Daniel Finn
articles.content_excerpt: There has been a virulent backlash in the British media against the Green Party of England and Wales since delegates at the party conference voted for a motion that brands Zionism as a racist ideology and supports the formation of a single democratic state in Palestine. As we have come to expect when British pundits and politicians are discussing Israel, nobody has seen fit to ask any Palestinians what they think about Zionism and what it has meant for them in practice. While Palestinians who live in Britain are studiously ignored, the media extends its search for critical voices to the rest of Europe. articles.title: Was Karl Kautsky Right About Ultra-Imperialism?
articles.author: Donald Parkinson
articles.content_excerpt: Six weeks after the outbreak of World War I, as Europe’s great empires sent millions to their deaths, Karl Kautsky published an essay predicting something almost impossible to believe. In an article for Die Neue Zeit called “Der Imperialismus,” better known under the English title “Ultra-Imperialism,” Kautsky argued that the leading powers were, despite all evidence to the contrary, moving toward not endless conflict but peaceful cooperation. The claim quickly came to seem absurd. As the trenches filled with corpses and the war consumed an entire generation, Kautsky’s essay looked less like a penetrating analysis than a spectacular misreading of history. articles.title: As Trump’s Coalition Breaks, Can the Left Pick Up the Pieces?
articles.author: Conor Lynch
articles.content_excerpt: The coalition that sent Donald Trump back to the White House in 2024 marked the culmination of a long-term political realignment that conservative authors and activists had anticipated since the 1970s. Fifty years earlier, right-wing commentators like William Rusher, then the publisher of National Review , were busy sketching a blueprint for the new majority that they hoped would finally bring them to power after decades of Democratic rule. That majority, according to Rusher and other “New Right” thinkers, would be built around the same working class that had long served as a pillar of the New Deal coalition. articles.title: “The Spanish People Will Remember Who Betrayed Them”
articles.author: Pablo Bustinduy
articles.content_excerpt: Could it be that Spain hasn’t let you know? None of you — none of you — is the person who has two weeks to find an apartment without knowing where they’ll go. And none of you is the person living in fear of an eviction notice arriving. None of you is the person counting the months until their lease ends, waiting for their landlord to say something. None of you is the person coming home from work today with the radio on to hear the result of this vote. None of you is one of those people, yet you are going to decide for them. You are going to decide what happens with their lives. articles.title: No, Digger Is Not a Misunderstood Masterpiece
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content_excerpt: You may have heard already that Digger , the new film cowritten and directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu ( The Revenant, Birdman ) and starring Tom Cruise, is an expensive box-office bomb that got many annihilating reviews . One of the better ones sums it up perfectly: “It’s like being trapped inside a tuba for two hours.” Bad news travels fast. And I’m going to further speed it along by providing an all-spoiler review, so consider yourself warned. This is in order to convince you that you’d be better off staying home watching Dr. Strangelove , Stanley Kubrick’s scathingly funny and incisive 1964 protest against world-ending insanity, which set the template for satirical black comedy for generations to come. articles.title: Lula Is in Danger of Losing Brazil’s Presidency
articles.author: Aldo Cordeiro Sauda
articles.content_excerpt: The first round of Brazil’s elections dealt a heavy blow to the Workers’ Party (PT) and, more broadly, to the cause of democracy in Latin America. In 2022, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva finished some six million votes ahead of Jair Bolsonaro in the first round, a margin that narrowed to about two million in the runoff. This time, Flávio Bolsonaro finished 2.2 million votes ahead of Lula, a lead of three percentage points. That makes the second round on October 25 especially difficult for Lula and the Brazilian left. The candidates who finished behind the top two, who together took around six million votes (roughly 6 percent), are all on the far right.
